english: They eat meatballs for lunch.
tip: Use till for what you eat at a meal: köttbullar till lunch = meatballs for lunch.

english: He works at a hospital.
tip: Jobba is the casual word for work, as in han jobbar. Arbeta means the same but sounds more formal.

english: I'm waiting for five minutes.
tip: I marks a span of time: väntar i fem minuter = wait for five minutes.

english: She needs a new computer.
tip: With an en-word the adjective stays base: en ny dator, but a neuter noun would force nytt.

english: We have fika at three.
tip: Fika is the Swedish coffee-and-cake break, both noun and verb: äter fika = have a fika.

english: He is a good cook.
tip: Professions drop the article (Han är kock), but add en once an adjective appears: en bra kock.

english: I would like water, please.
tip: To want a thing, add ha: vill ha vatten = want water. Vill alone only pairs with another verb.

english: One, two, three, four, five.
tip: Counting up: en, två, tre, fyra, fem. Watch två, said 'tvoo' with the å like the o in 'more'.

english: A plate of meatballs, please.
tip: A container of something uses med: en tallrik med köttbullar = a plate of meatballs.

english: We sit down at the table.
tip: Sätta sig means sit down and is reflexive: Vi sätter oss uses oss for we.

english: I do laundry every other day.
tip: Varannan means every other: tvättar kläder varannan dag = every other day.

english: I take the bus to school.
tip: Taking transport uses the definite: tar bussen = take the bus, literally take the-bus.

english: I drink a glass of water.
tip: A glass of water needs no linking word: ett glas vatten, the two nouns just sit together.

english: The bus comes every fifteen minutes.
tip: var before a time unit means 'every': var femtonde minut = every fifteen minutes.

english: We drink light beer with the food.
tip: Lättöl is one word from lätt (light) plus öl (beer); Swedish freely glues nouns together.

target: Jag arbetar på ett stort kontor.
english: I work at a large office.
tip: A neuter (ett) noun forces -t on the adjective: ett stort kontor, not stor.

target: De tittar på TV på kvällen.
english: They watch television in the evening.
tip: Titta needs på to watch something: tittar på TV = watch TV.

target: Vi tycker att filmen var bra.
english: We think the movie was good.
tip: tycker states an opinion or taste; use tror for belief or a guess: vi tycker att filmen var bra.

target: Vi möter våra vänner på lördag.
english: We meet our friends on Saturday.
tip: På lördag means this coming Saturday; add -ar (på lördagar) for every Saturday.

target: Jag dricker alltid kaffe till frukosten.
english: I always drink coffee with breakfast.
tip: Adverbs like alltid sit right after the verb in a main clause: dricker alltid kaffe.

target: Jag vill ha socker i teet.
english: I want sugar in the tea.
tip: Te (tea) becomes teet once the definite ending is added: socker i teet = sugar in the tea.

target: Jag lyssnar på musik på tåget.
english: I listen to music on the train.
tip: Lyssna takes på before what you hear: lyssnar på musik = listen to music.

target: Vi äter frukost klockan halv åtta.
english: We eat breakfast at half past seven.
tip: Halv åtta means 7:30, not 8:30. Swedish counts toward the next hour, so it is literally half to eight.

target: Vi behöver byta tåg i Nässjö.
english: We need to change trains in Nässjö.
tip: Byta means change or switch: byta tåg = change trains, with no article on tåg.

target: Hon är duktig på att laga mat.
english: She is good at cooking.
tip: Duktig takes på att before a verb: duktig på att laga mat = good at cooking.

target: Jag har en bror och en syster.
english: I have a brother and a sister.
tip: Swedish repeats the article for each noun: en bror och en syster, not one en for both.

target: Det borde gå bra just nu också.
english: It should be fine right now too.
tip: borde (should) is a modal, so the next verb is a plain infinitive with no att: borde gå bra.

english: The bistro car has good food.
tip: God means good-tasting for food, while bra is good in general: god mat = tasty food.

english: It is the fifteenth of March.
tip: Ordinal dates use -e or -te endings: femtonde = fifteenth. Swedish dates go day-month.

english: We eat dinner at six o'clock.
tip: Middag looks like English 'midday' but means dinner, the evening meal, as in vi äter middag klockan sex.
